title: Sample-optimal learning of stabilizer states
authors: Rebecca Chang, Matthias C. Caro, Martin Larocca, Maxwell West
abstract: It is well-known that learning a pure $n$-qubit stabilizer state $|ψ\rangle$ both requires, and can be accomplished with, access to a number of copies of $|ψ\rangle$ linear in $n$. However, the precise constant coefficient of this scaling does not appear to have been determined. Here we prove that $L_δ(n)$, the smallest number of copies from which a quantum procedure can identify any stabilizer state with failure probability at most $0<δ<1/8$, satisfies $n+\lceil\log_2(1/δ)\rceil-3\leq L_δ(n)\leq n+\left\lceil\log_2(1/δ)\right\rceil+4$. We present a polynomial-time quantum learning algorithm that saturates this bound, achieving a constant factor improvement in sample-complexity over previously known approaches. As an immediate corollary, we obtain via the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism an algorithm for learning an unknown $n$-qubit Clifford unitary from $2n+\left\lceil\log_2(1/δ)\right\rceil+4$ queries, the $n$-dependence of which we show to be optimal. Our proof technique, which involves Fourier analysis on the abelian group $\mathbb{Z}_4^n \times \mathbb{F}_2^{n(n-1)/2}$, seems to be qualitatively different to previous approaches to stabilizer state learning, and may be of some independent interest; in particular, it admits natural generalisations to further problems in quantum learning theory.
summary: This paper provides a rigorous determination of the sample complexity required to learn an unknown n-qubit stabilizer state. It introduces a novel, efficient quantum algorithm that achieves the optimal scaling for this task. The work is significant for quantum information theory as it provides tight bounds and a practical method for characterizing quantum states.
main_problem: The paper determines the minimum number of copies required to learn an unknown pure n-qubit stabilizer state and subsequently derives the complexity for learning associated Clifford unitaries.
main_result: They establish tight bounds for the sample complexity, $L_\delta(n) \approx n + \log(1/\delta)$, and present a polynomial-time quantum algorithm that saturates these bounds.
method: The approach uses a multi-stage quantum algorithm involving reduction to a full-support state, isotypic compression, and applying the Quantum Fourier Transform over a specific abelian group structure.
model_or_system: The system under study is the $n$-qubit stabilizer state, which are specific quantum states generated by the Clifford group acting on computational basis states.
key_observables: The primary observable is the sample complexity, $L_\delta(n)$, which quantifies the minimum number of state copies needed for successful identification.
important_parameters: The key parameters are the number of qubits ($n$), the failure probability ($\delta$), and the structure of the underlying abelian group $\Upsilon$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the ability to implement random Clifford operations and relies on bounding probabilities using techniques like the Hellinger overlap.
figures_summary: Figure 1 provides an overview of the four core stages of the proposed stabilizer-learning algorithm, detailing the sequence of operations from state reduction to tableau reconstruction.
paper_structure: The paper follows a logical progression: first, establishing the problem bounds; second, detailing the four-stage quantum algorithm (reduction, compression, Fourier transform, reconstruction); and finally, analyzing the computational complexity of each step.
why_interesting: While focused on quantum computation, the rigorous analysis of state learning complexity and the use of Fourier analysis on group structures provide deep theoretical tools applicable to characterizing entanglement and resource estimation in quantum many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of our stabilizer-learning algorithm, which has four core stages. In stage one we reduce the problem to that of learning a stabilizer state which has support on all computational basis strings; such “full-rank” states enjoy certain nice algebraic properties which we are able to exploit. In particular, they are exactly the orbit on the state |+⟩⊗n of a certain representation of the abelian group Υ ∼= Zn 4 × F n(n−1)/2 2 . The test (correctly) rejecting a rank-deficient state is non-destructive, so that the test can be uncomputed and another trial performed; the test (incorrectly) rejecting a full-support causes the algorithm to fail (not depicted in the figure).
